Integrates with `consoleStore` (new additive slice), `ShockPanel` (one mount point), `shocks.ts` (unchanged, consumed via `applyTwist`), and leaves E3 to own all weather animation (the loading affordance here is the plain "reading the sky" label only). ### Component Breakdown | Component | Responsibility | File | |-----------|---------------|------| | Shock parse boundary | Schema, system prompt, request builder, fetch wrapper with 3 s timeout, 5 step validation pipeline, type guard, hash cache, ShockSpec adapters | src/lib/shockParse.ts | | Parse tests | Clamp table, percent detect, rejects, timeout, 429 no retry, cache hit, chip steps, request shape, no key | src/lib/shockParse.test.ts | | Dash content guard | Dash rule scan for the new src/lib files (dashScan.test.ts left untouched) | src/lib/shockParse.dash.test.ts | | Typed shock row | "Say the shock" input, mode badge, "reading the sky" loading, inline fallback note | src/components/console/TypedShock.tsx | | Confirmation chips | Per parameter chips with one click steppers, formula strip, confirm (button or Enter), discard | src/components/console/ShockChips.tsx | | UI smoke test | jsdom end to end typed flow plus fallback flow with mocked fetch | src/components/console/typedShock.smoke.test.ts | | Store slice | typedStatus, pendingShock, typedNote, shockMode + 4 new actions, backward compatible | src/state/consoleStore.ts | | Store tests | Confirm gate, fallback notes, chip correction, reset clearing (new file, E2 tests untouched) | src/state/consoleStore.typed.test.ts | | Styles | Mode badge, chips, formula strip, note, reduced motion guards | src/index.css (appended cp- block) | | Key plumbing | Env placeholder and gitignore rules | .env.example, .gitignore | **Placement decision (UI in `src/components/console/`, not `src/components/gemini/`)**: (1) `src/state` and `src/components/console` are the dashScan auto-scanned directories, so new console components inherit the content rule enforcement for free; (2) the typed row is console surface UI mounted inside `ShockPanel`, and E2 layering keeps one folder per view; (3) a new folder would fall outside both the dash scan auto dirs and the documented frontend layering map. Trade-off: `src/lib` is not auto-scanned, so the two new lib files get their own small guard test instead of editing `dashScan.test.ts` (which must not be modified). ### Data Flow ``` "laid off and rent up 15%" + PromptMetrics(profile) | v parseShockSentence -- cacheKeyFor(accountId, hash(normalized sentence)) | |-- hit: return cached ParseOutcome (no fetch) | |-- no VITE_GEMINI_KEY: rejected no_key (no fetch) v fetch v1beta generateContent (x-goog-api-key, responseSchema, temperature 0, maxOutputTokens 300, thinkingLevel minimal, store false, AbortSignal.timeout(3000)) | v envelope text -> JSON.parse -> type guard -> percent detect -> clamp -> round -> reject rules (validateShockPayload) | v ParseOutcome = ok(spec, summary, confidence, fixes) | rejected(reason) | timeout | +-- ok -> consoleStore.parseTypedShock -> typedStatus 'pending' | pendingShock (twist state UNTOUCHED, runway does not move) | | | v | ShockChips: steppers (applySpecStep) + shockFormula dollars strip | | | v confirmTypedShock (click or Enter) | twist = normalizeTwist(shockSpecToTwist(spec)) <-- ONE consumer | activePresetId = matchPreset(twist), shockMode 'gemini' | +-- rejected/timeout -> typedStatus 'fallback', typedNote (reason mapped) shockMode 'preset', preset cards stay rendered and clickable ``` ### File Structure | File | Purpose | Changes | |------|---------|---------| | src/lib/shockParse.ts | Typed boundary module (everything below) | New | | src/lib/shockParse.test.ts | Unit tests, mocked fetch, no network at test time | New | | src/lib/shockParse.dash.test.ts | Dash scan over shockParse.ts and shockParse.test.ts | New | | src/components/console/TypedShock.tsx | Input row + mode badge + loading label + fallback note | New; mounted by ShockPanel | | src/components/console/ShockChips.tsx | Pending chips + formula strip + confirm gate | New; rendered by TypedShock | | src/components/console/typedShock.smoke.test.ts | jsdom smoke tests | New | | src/components/console/ShockPanel.tsx | Mount `` directly above `cp-presets` | 1 line added, no behavior change to E2 paths | | src/state/consoleStore.ts | Additive typed slice + 4 actions; applyPreset/reset/selectAccount also clear typed state and abort in flight parses | Extended, E2 actions unchanged | | src/state/consoleStore.typed.test.ts | New tests for the slice | New | | src/index.css | Append cp- badge/chip/formula/note styles; motion wrapped in `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` | Appended | | .env.example | `VITE_GEMINI_KEY=` placeholder (committed) | New | | .gitignore | Add `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.*.local` | Appended | | docs/architecture.md | Append "### Implementation layout" inside the Gemini section (exact text below) | Appended | | docs/decisions.md | Append decision record (exact text below) | Appended | ### Technology Decisions | Decision | Choice | Why | Alternative Rejected | Trade-off | |----------|--------|-----|---------------------|-----------| | HTTP client | Plain `fetch`, header `x-goog-api-key` | Settled; SDK sends Api-Revision header failing CORS preflight 403 | @google/genai SDK | Hand maintained request body | | Model | `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` constant | Settled list; lite is fastest for a constrained JSON mapping, thinkingLevel minimal | gemini-3.6-flash | If 3.5 lite misparses at rehearsal, the constant flips in one place | | Validation | Hand written type guard + pure pipeline | No zod allowed; matches profiles.ts strictness culture | zod | More code, fully pinned by tests | | Timeout | `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)` combined with caller signal via small `combineSignals` helper | Settled hard cap; manual combine avoids `AbortSignal.any` typing/runtime risk | AbortSignal.any | A few lines of listener wiring | | Payload money unit | Whole integer cents in the user prompt with one clarifying line; system instruction stays unit free | Brief blesses cents as whole numbers; integers keep the exactness contract; the clarifying line prevents a 100x oneOff error, and clamp + confirm strip catch residue | Dollars in the prompt | Model must do one dollars to cents step | | Cache key | `accountId + ':' + fnv1a(normalized sentence)`, successes only, 32 entry cap | oneOffMonths is derived through account spending, so sentence alone can misparse across accounts | Sentence only key | Retyping after switching accounts costs one call (still correct) | | Formula strip math | `shockFormula()` calls `applyTwist` + `scaleCents`, returns cents terms; component only formats | The strip can never disagree with the runway number | Computing terms in JSX | Reuses E2 math, no duplication | | Confirmation state | `pendingShock` in store, `twist` untouched until confirm | Settled mandatory gate; derived runway in ConsoleView reads `twist`, so the gate is structural | Apply-then-undo | Pending lives one click from applied | | Percent detection scope | `incomeFactor` and `billsPct` only | These are the fraction fields; `oneOffMonths` (0 to 12) and `durationMonths` (0 to 120) legitimately exceed 1, dividing them would destroy valid parses | All numeric fields | Documents the one place the settled wording needed field scoping | | Dash enforcement | New guard test for new lib files | dashScan.test.ts must not be modified | Adding paths to dashScan EXPLICIT_FILES | Slight duplication of scan logic | ### Interfaces **src/lib/shockParse.ts (the typed boundary, complete export surface):** ```ts export const GEMINI_MODEL = 'gemini-3.5-flash-lite' export const PARSE_TIMEOUT_MS = 3000 export type ShockIntent = 'job_loss' | 'bills_up' | 'one_off_cost' | 'mixed' | 'no_shock' export type ShockConfidence = 'high' | 'medium' | 'low' /** The shared shock spec: 3 math fields + display only horizon. */ export interface ShockSpec { incomeFactor: number // 0..1, 2 dp billsPct: number // 0..1, 2 dp oneOffMonths: number // 0..12, 1 dp durationMonths: number // 0..120 integer, display only } export interface ShockPayload extends ShockSpec { intent: ShockIntent confidence: ShockConfidence summary: string } export interface PromptMetrics { accountId: string incomeCents: number fixedCostsCents: number spendingCents: number bufferCents: number householdBillsCents: number loanPaymentCents: number runwayMonths: number // runway_deci_months / 10 } export type ParseFixField = 'incomeFactor' | 'billsPct' | 'oneOffMonths' | 'durationMonths' | 'summary' export interface ParseFix { field: ParseFixField; fix: 'percent' | 'clamp' | 'round' } export type RejectReason = | 'empty_input' | 'no_key' | 'malformed_json' | 'bad_shape' | 'no_shock' | 'low_confidence' | 'all_neutral' | 'rate_limited' | 'http_error' | 'network_error' | 'aborted' export type ParseOutcome = | { kind: 'ok'; spec: ShockSpec; intent: ShockIntent; confidence: 'high' | 'medium'; summary: string; fixes: ParseFix[] } | { kind: 'rejected'; reason: RejectReason; detail: string } | { kind: 'timeout' } export function parseShockSentence( sentence: string, metrics: PromptMetrics, signal?: AbortSignal, ): Promise export function isShockPayload(raw: unknown): raw is ShockPayload export function validateShockPayload(raw: unknown): | { ok: true; spec: ShockSpec; intent: ShockIntent; confidence: ShockConfidence; summary: string; fixes: ParseFix[] } | { ok: false; reason: RejectReason; detail: string } export function promptMetrics(profile: AccountProfile): PromptMetrics export function shockSpecToTwist(spec: ShockSpec): Partial export function applySpecStep(spec: ShockSpec, field: 'incomeFactor' | 'billsPct' | 'oneOffMonths' | 'durationMonths', delta: number): ShockSpec export interface ShockFormula { incomeAfterCents: number billsDeltaCents: number spendingAfterCents: number oneOffCents: number bufferLeftCents: number } export function shockFormula(profile: AccountProfile, spec: ShockSpec): ShockFormula export function normalizeSentence(sentence: string): string export function hashSentence(sentence: string): string // fnv1a 32 bit, 8 hex chars export function cacheKeyFor(sentence: string, accountId: string): string export function clearShockParseCache(): void export function shockParseCacheSize(): number ``` **Validation pipeline (exact semantics, in architecture order 1 to 5):** 1. Envelope: `candidates[0].content.parts[].text` joined; missing envelope -> `bad_shape`. `JSON.parse` in try/catch -> `malformed_json`. 2. `isShockPayload`: plain object with exactly the 7 keys, `intent` and `confidence` in enum, 4 finite numbers (`Number.isFinite`), non empty string summary. Extra or missing key -> `bad_shape`. 3. Percent detect (incomeFactor and billsPct only): if `1 < x <= 100`, `x = x / 100`, fix `percent`. 4. Clamp: incomeFactor and billsPct to [0, 1]; oneOffMonths to [0, 12]; durationMonths rounded to integer then [0, 120]; fix `clamp` on change. 5. Round: incomeFactor 2 dp, billsPct 2 dp, oneOffMonths 1 dp (fix `round` on change); summary sliced to 90 chars (fix `clamp` on truncation). Then reject: `intent === 'no_shock'` -> `no_shock`; `confidence === 'low'` -> `low_confidence`; `incomeFactor === 1 && billsPct === 0 && oneOffMonths === 0` -> `all_neutral`. **shockSpecToTwist (presets and typed path converge here):** ```ts { jobLoss: spec.incomeFactor < 1, incomeFactor: spec.incomeFactor, billsDeltaPct: Math.round(spec.billsPct * 100), oneOffMonthsTenths: Math.round(spec.oneOffMonths * 10), extraMonthlyCents: 0, durationMonths: spec.durationMonths, } ``` 2 dp fractions map exactly onto Twist's quantization (whole percents, whole tenths), so no precision is lost at the boundary. **Request (plain fetch, exact body):** ```ts POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/gemini-3.5-flash-lite:generateContent headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'x-goog-api-key': key } body: { contents: [{ role: 'user', parts: [{ text: userPrompt }] }], systemInstruction: { parts: [{ text: SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION }] }, generationConfig: { temperature: 0, maxOutputTokens: 300, responseMimeType: 'application/json', responseSchema: SHOCK_RESPONSE_SCHEMA, thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel: 'minimal' }, }, store: false, } ``` `responseSchema`: object, `additionalProperties: false`, all 7 in `required` and `propertyOrdering`, `intent` and `confidence` as enums, `incomeFactor`/`billsPct` number 0..1, `oneOffMonths` number 0..12, `durationMonths` integer 0..120, `summary` string maxLength 90. **SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION (unit free, no customer data):** > You map one short financial shock sentence to structured shock parameters for a resilience calculator. Return only the JSON object the schema requires, no markdown, no extra keys. Field meanings, all unit free: intent is job_loss, bills_up, one_off_cost, mixed, or no_shock; use no_shock when the sentence describes no change at all. incomeFactor is the fraction of usual monthly income the customer keeps, 0 to 1, use 1 when income is unchanged; when income stops and a benefit replaces a stated share of it, use that share (a benefit covering 55 percent means 0.55), and when income stops with no benefit stated, use 0. billsPct is the fractional rise in household bills, 0 to 1 (15 percent up is 0.15), use 0 when bills are unchanged. oneOffMonths is a one off cost expressed in months of typical spending, 0 to 12, use 0 when there is none. durationMonths is an integer count of months the change lasts, 0 to 120, display only, use 0 when the sentence gives no duration or implies a permanent change. confidence is high when the mapping is clear, medium when you had to assume, low when the sentence is ambiguous or not about money. summary restates the mapped shock in plain words, at most 90 characters. Rules: the fields are fractions and counts, never money. The user message carries the customer's baseline figures as plain numbers; use them only to turn amounts named in the sentence into oneOffMonths of spending. Never copy customer data into the summary. Percents in the sentence always become fraction values here. **User prompt template:** ``` Map this shock sentence. sentence: "" account_id: "" baseline: {"income": , "fixed_costs": , "spending": , "buffer": , "household_bills": , "loan_payment":

, "runway_months": } The six money figures are cents and amounts in the sentence are dollars, so 2000 dollars is 200000 cents. ``` No raw rows, no history, no checksum, nothing else (test asserts the body text excludes `balance_series`, `check_sum`, `history`). **consoleStore additions (backward compatible; E2 fields and actions untouched):** ```ts export type TypedShockStatus = 'idle' | 'reading' | 'pending' | 'fallback' export type ShockMode = 'preset' | 'gemini' export interface PendingShock { sentence: string spec: ShockSpec intent: ShockIntent confidence: 'high' | 'medium' summary: string fixes: ParseFix[] } // new state (defaults: 'idle', null, null, 'preset') typedStatus: TypedShockStatus pendingShock: PendingShock | null typedNote: string | null shockMode: ShockMode // new actions parseTypedShock: (sentence: string) => Promise // aborts any in flight parse (generation counter), sets 'reading', calls parseShockSentence with promptMetrics(profile); ok -> 'pending' + pendingShock; rejected/timeout -> 'fallback' + reason mapped typedNote confirmTypedShock: () => void // twist = normalizeTwist(shockSpecToTwist(pendingShock.spec)); activePresetId = matchPreset(twist); shockMode 'gemini'; clears pending and note adjustPendingShock: (field: 'incomeFactor' | 'billsPct' | 'oneOffMonths' | 'durationMonths', delta: number) => void // applySpecStep then re store; steps: 0.05 / 0.01 / 0.1 / 1 cancelTypedShock: () => void ``` Existing `applyPreset` and `resetTwist`/`resetAll` additionally clear typed state, set `shockMode` to 'preset', and abort in flight parses; `selectAccount` clears typed state (account switch invalidates a pending parse). Existing consoleStore tests assert only pre existing fields, so they stay green. **Components:** - `TypedShock.tsx` props `{ profile: AccountProfile }`. Renders label "Say the shock", input `id="shock-sentence"` (Enter submits), button "Read the sky", mode badge (`"typed shock Gemini"` when `shockMode === 'gemini'`, else `"preset cards"`), `role="status"` "reading the sky" while `typedStatus === 'reading'`, and the fallback note when `typedStatus === 'fallback'`. Renders `` when `typedStatus === 'pending'`. - `ShockChips.tsx` props `{ profile: AccountProfile; pending: PendingShock }`. One chip per parameter (income keeps percent, bills percent, one off months of spending, horizon months) each with one click minus/plus steppers via `adjustPendingShock`; formula strip from `shockFormula(profile, pending.spec)` formatted with `formatCents` (lines: `Income: {p}% of {I} = {incomeAfter}`, `Spending: {S} + {p}% of bills {H} = {spendingAfter}`, `One off: {m} months of spending = {oneOff} from the buffer`, `Buffer left: {bufferLeft}`); "Apply shock" button auto focused on mount (Enter confirms) plus a ghost "Discard". No arithmetic in JSX. **CSS (appended to src/index.css):** `--cp-badge-gemini: var(--cp-band-fair)` token; classes `.cp-typed`, `.cp-typed__row`, `.cp-typed__input`, `.cp-mode-badge`, `.cp-mode-badge-gemini`, `.cp-reading`, `.cp-chips`, `.cp-chip`, `.cp-chip__stepper`, `.cp-formula`, `.cp-formula__line`, `.cp-note`, `.cp-note-fallback`. Any transition or opacity pulse wrapped in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)` with the reduce branch disabling it. No new animation beyond that. **State model, confirmation and fallback (explicit):** - Parsed but unconfirmed = `typedStatus 'pending'` with `pendingShock` set. `twist` is not written, so ConsoleView's `useMemo` derivation (runway, verdict, plan) is structurally frozen at the pre parse numbers until `confirmTypedShock`. This is the mandatory misparse guard. - Chips allow one click correction per parameter through `applySpecStep` (clamped and re rounded through the same helpers the pipeline uses) before confirm; the formula strip shows the dollars arithmetic the judge hand verifies. - Fallback: `typedStatus 'fallback'`, `shockMode 'preset'`, preset cards remain rendered and clickable (they always are), no auto apply of any preset. - Mode badge values: `"typed shock Gemini"` only after a confirmed typed shock; `"preset cards"` otherwise and after every failure. - Inline note mapping: `no_key` -> "Gemini key not configured, using preset cards"; `timeout`/`rate_limited`/`http_error`/`network_error`/`aborted` -> "Gemini unavailable, using preset cards"; model side (`malformed_json`/`bad_shape`/`no_shock`/`low_confidence`/`all_neutral`/`empty_input`) -> "No clear shock in that sentence, using preset cards". - Hash cache: `cacheKeyFor = accountId + ':' + fnv1a(normalizeSentence(sentence))`, successes only, 32 entries FIFO; a cache hit is free (no fetch) and the console.info log records `{ hash, latency ms, raw JSON, clamped JSON, cached: true }` for the write-up p50. ### Implementation status and delegation **Nothing was implemented on disk and no verification command was run**: this session exposes no write/edit tool and no shell tool (tool discovery exhausted; only read/grep/glob and non-repo API tools exist). Also unperformed for the same reason: the Knowledge Sharing step (appending "### Implementation layout" to docs/architecture.md and the decision record to docs/decisions.md). Exact text for both appends is in the next section for whoever executes. Both must keep: no em dashes or double hyphens, no new dependencies, no E2 test edits, no E3 to E7 mounts, no real key in any file, mocked fetch in tests. ### Test matrix (all required cases, mapped) | Required case | Where | |---------------|-------| | Clamp table (bounds and fixes) | shockParse.test.ts `validateShockPayload` table | | Percent detection (1 boundary, 100, above 100, exempt fields) | shockParse.test.ts | | Reject: no_shock, low confidence, all neutral, malformed JSON, missing/wrong/extra fields | shockParse.test.ts | | Timeout (real 3 s abort test plus simulated TimeoutError mapping) | shockParse.test.ts | | 429 no retry fallback (fetch called once) and 403 | shockParse.test.ts | | Hash cache hit (fetch once, deep equal outcome; different account refetches) | shockParse.test.ts | | Chip correction produces corrected ShockSpec (`applySpecStep`) | shockParse.test.ts | | Request shape (URL, key header, schema, thinkingLevel, store false, temperature 0, 300 tokens, no raw rows in body) | shockParse.test.ts | | Graceful no key (rejected `no_key`, fetch never called) | shockParse.test.ts | | specToTwist mapping and shockFormula vs applyTwist cross check | shockParse.test.ts | | Confirm gate: twist and applyTwist output unchanged until confirm | consoleStore.typed.test.ts | | Fallback note per reason, mode badge state, reset clearing, abort on account switch | consoleStore.typed.test.ts | | UI end to end typed flow and fallback flow | typedShock.smoke.test.ts | ### Verification Checklist - [x] All components have clear responsibilities (table above) - [x] Data flow is complete (no dead ends; every failure lands on preset cards) - [x] File structure follows project conventions (pure lib + store + console components, cp- tokens) - [x] Technology choices justified (table above) - [x] Risks identified with mitigations (unit confusion: clamp + confirm strip; exact counts to be reported) — **not run** - [ ] `npm run build` PASS — **not run** ### Docs text to append (verbatim) **docs/architecture.md**, at the end of "## Gemini shock input" after "### Fit with hard constraints" (do not rewrite settled content): ```markdown ### Implementation layout Files: src/lib/shockParse.ts (response schema, system prompt, plain fetch wrapper with the 3 second AbortSignal timeout, the five step validation pipeline, the hand written type guard, the hash cache, the ShockSpec to Twist adapter, and the formula terms) with shockParse.test.ts and shockParse.dash.test.ts; src/components/console/TypedShock.tsx (input row, mode badge, reading the sky label, fallback note) and ShockChips.tsx (confirmation chips with steppers, formula strip, confirm gate) with typedShock.smoke.test.ts; src/state/consoleStore.ts gains a typed slice (typedStatus, pendingShock, typedNote, shockMode plus parseTypedShock, confirmTypedShock, adjustPendingShock, cancelTypedShock) with consoleStore.typed.test.ts; src/index.css appends cp- badge, chip, formula and note styles; .env.example plus .env gitignore rules for VITE_GEMINI_KEY. Console components live in src/components/console so the dash scan auto dirs cover them. Typed boundary: parseShockSentence(sentence, metrics, signal) returns a ParseOutcome union of ok (ShockSpec plus summary, confidence, and fix flags), rejected (reason), or timeout. shockSpecToTwist maps the shared ShockSpec onto the E2 Twist (jobLoss is incomeFactor below 1, billsDeltaPct is round(billsPct x 100), oneOffMonthsTenths is round(oneOffMonths x 10), extraMonthlyCents 0), so the preset path and the typed path share one consumer: store twist state feeding applyTwist. Confirmation model: a parsed shock is pendingShock state, never twist state, so the runway cannot move until confirmTypedShock. Chips step each field through applySpecStep (clamped and re rounded) and the formula strip renders shockFormula dollars arithmetic; the confirm button is auto focused so Enter confirms. Failure model: any rejected or timeout outcome sets typedStatus fallback with a reason mapped note (no key: Gemini key not configured, using preset cards; timeout or network: Gemini unavailable, using preset cards; model side: No clear shock in that sentence, using preset cards) and the mode badge reads preset cards while the preset cards stay clickable. The hash cache key is the FNV hash of the normalized sentence namespaced by account id, because one off amounts convert through that account's spending. ``` **docs/decisions.md**, appended entry: ```markdown ## Nov 07 2026 - Gemini shock input: typed path with mandatory confirm **Context**: the gated Gemini add-on maps a typed shock sentence onto the same Twist the preset cards feed. A misparse visible to a judge computing by hand is the worst failure mode, and the network path must never be a dependency. **Decision**: src/lib/shockParse.ts owns the boundary (plain fetch, gemini-3.5-flash-lite, responseSchema, 3 second AbortSignal timeout, five step validation, hash cache keyed on sentence plus account id). A parsed shock is pendingShock store state only; the twist (and therefore the runway) is written solely by confirmTypedShock after chip review with a hand verifiable dollars formula strip. All failures degrade to the always live preset cards with a reason mapped note. Prompt carries the sentence, account_id, and six judge metrics as plain integer cents (user approved the identifier leaving the browser, Nov 07 2026). **Rationale**: the confirm gate makes a misparse structurally unable to reach state; cents integers keep the exactness contract and a single clarifying prompt line plus clamps and the formula strip bound any unit error. **Trade-offs**: a sentence reused across accounts refetches (correctness over cache hits); percent detection applies to incomeFactor and billsPct only since the two count fields legitimately exceed 1; the stretch mic input is not built. ``` ### Deliberately left out Web Speech mic input (stretch, 1 to 1.5 h), any weather animation (E3 owns it), auto applying a preset on fallback (the presenter chooses, the cards are always live), caching failure outcomes (a transient 429 must not stick), and any change to `shocks.ts`, E2 tests, `dashScan.test.ts`, `scripts/`, or E3 to E7 mounts. ### Test results Not available: `npm run typecheck`, `npx vitest run`, and `npm run build` could not be executed in this session (no shell tool). ## Acceptance gate: 7/7 green

|---|---------|--------|
| 1 | `npm install` | rc=0 |

| 7 | `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify` | **PASS**, drift none, sha256 `9ec428bf...` |

Migration gate is closed and green. Note the last command is `scripts.engine.verify`, not the runbook's old `scripts.analysis.verify_findings` (that was the pre-pivot pipeline).

## Deploy to Pages + custom domain

**Critical trap first:** `deploy.yml` currently builds with `VITE_BASE=/stormfund/` because this is a project Pages site. The moment you attach a custom domain, GitHub serves your site from the **root** (`/`), so every asset would 404. The workflow's base logic only special-cases `*.github.io` repos, and its asset verification greps for `stormfund/assets/`. Both must learn about CNAME before the domain goes live, or the first deploy with the domain breaks.

**The sequence (your steps are browser-side, mine are code-side):**

1. **Push** (mine, needs your go): current commits + Entire checkpoints ride along, first Actions run builds and deploys to `https://ajeet-krish.github.io/stormfund/`
2. **Enable Pages** (you, if the auto-enablement does not fire): Settings → Pages → Source: **GitHub Actions**
3. **Fix `deploy.yml`** (mine, before the domain is attached): treat a committed `CNAME` file (or `PAGES_BASE_PATH=/`) as `base="/"`, and make the asset check accept both forms
4. **DNS at your registrar** (you): create a **CNAME record**, host `www`, value `ajeet-krish.github.io` (runbook rule: use a subdomain, apex needs four A records and is more fragile; TTL default is fine, fresh records resolve in minutes to a few hours)
5. **Attach domain** (you): Settings → Pages → Custom domain → enter `www.<yourdomain>` → Save. GitHub runs its DNS check
6. **Verify** (you or me): `dig www.<yourdomain> +noall +answer -t CNAME` must return `ajeet-krish.github.io` before you trust it
7. **Enforce HTTPS** (you): checkbox appears once DNS resolves, can take up to 24 hours to become available
8. **Commit the CNAME** (me, if GitHub does not create it): the file must exist in the repo so future builds know to use `base="/"`

Fallback if anything stalls: the `github.io` URL keeps working and does not block submission (runbook rule).

See your money move like weather.

Storm Fund is a resilience financial engine that visualizes a bank account as a real-time weather forecast. Anonymized bank data maps runway and buffer to a pixel sky. Inject a shock and watch the forecast change.

## Screenshot

## Primary Features

1. **Account Runway Analysis**: Income, fixed costs, spending, savings buffer, household bills, loan payment, and months of runway for any account_id.
2. **Shock Simulator**: Apply a job loss with EI, a furnace repair, a bills increase, or any mix, and recompute runway live.
3. **Make a plan**: Build an emergency fund goal plan and a shock backup plan based on the account's numbers.

## Demo video

*[Placeholder: link to the 2 minute demo video]*

## Full Feature breakdown

### Know the customer: account profile

Search any of the 4,500 account_ids in the dataset and the console loads a precomputed baseline profile: income (I), fixed costs (F), spending (S), savings buffer (B), household bills (H), and loan payment (P), each computed with the exact definitions from the challenge brief (median of money_in, median of money_out, mean of avg_daily_balance over the last 6 months, and so on). Every number carries a provenance stamp naming its source file and rows, and the profile loader refuses schema drift instead of guessing.

Everything is precomputed offline into `public/data/engine/profiles.json`, so any account answers instantly with zero network calls, which is what makes the live judging format (a judge picks an account you have never seen) safe.

### Take a shock: shock simulator

Three one-click twist cards reproduce the brief's example shocks: job loss with EI at 55 percent, a furnace repair costing one full month of typical spending, and the combined job loss plus household bills up 15 percent. Sliders let you change the size of any shock (EI replacement rate, bills increase, one-off cost).

The runway formula runs in integer cents with the exact branch order from the brief: buffer left after one-off costs, monthly gap between shocked spending and shocked income, runway of 0 when the buffer is gone, "no shortfall (120+)" as its own state when income covers spending, otherwise months capped at 120 and rounded to one decimal. The TypeScript implementation is validated against the Python pipeline's golden fixtures and a cross-check of all 4,500 profiles, so the number on screen and the number a judge computes by hand agree.

A verdict band (clear to storm warning) summarizes the result, and the mode badge always shows where the input came from: preset cards or a typed sentence.

### Make a plan

Two plans derived from the customer's own numbers: an emergency fund goal plan (target, monthly contribution, months to goal) and a shock backup plan (whether they make it through the shock horizon, with fixed costs and the loan payment named as the cut floor). The plan formulas are our own declared definitions, permitted by the brief, and are stated on screen rather than hidden.

### Weather station visualization

A pure `weatherState` function maps the judge metrics onto seven weather states (clear, cloudy, overcast, rain, drought, storm, flood) with a printed mapping legend, so the skin stays honest: every visual element has a declared data rule behind it. The forecast strip shows the 12 month outlook with an EI-cliff overlay marking when benefits run out, weather bands render the sky, and the severity ladder follows the Canadian yellow, orange, red alert order. Colors are colorblind safe (Okabe-Ito base), severity is carried by color plus icon plus text label together, and every animation respects prefers-reduced-motion.

### Typed shock input

Instead of preset buttons, type the shock in plain language ("they lose their job, EI covers half, and the furnace dies next month"). The input maps to the same structured shock parameters the presets use, shows them as confirmation chips you can correct with one click, and displays the dollar arithmetic in a formula strip so you can hand verify it before anything applies. The runway never changes until you confirm. Full details in the next section.

### Storm Atlas

### Solana receipt badge

## Use of Solana

## Use of Gemini API

The Gemini API powers the typed shock input. One structured request maps a free-form sentence to the exact shock parameters the calculator uses, with a strict JSON response schema so the output shape is guaranteed: intent (job loss, bills up, one-off cost, mixed, or no shock), income factor, bills percentage, one-off cost in months of spending, and duration.

The integration is built to be honest and safe rather than impressive-looking:

- **The model is a parser, not an oracle.** It never computes runway. Its output is clamped, percent-corrected, and type-checked in TypeScript, then shown as confirmation chips. The rules engine does all math, and the runway does not move until a human clicks apply.
- **The formula strip shows the dollars.** Before confirming, you see income and spending arithmetic in plain numbers, so a misparse is visible and correctable in one click, which matters when a judge may be computing the same number by hand.
- **Graceful failure is designed in.** Three second timeout, no retry on rate limits, and preset twist cards stay clickable at all times. If the key or the network is missing, the console says so and falls back without breaking the demo.
- **Privacy boundary.** The prompt carries the sentence, the account id, and six aggregate baseline figures as plain numbers. No raw rows, no transaction history, no customer data beyond that ever leaves the browser.

Built for the Sheridan Datathon 2026 (November 7 to 8) on the Tangerine track, "Resilience Rewired": a financial resilience engine that knows the customer, takes a shock, and makes a plan, demonstrated live against real anonymized bank data.

input.newString:
### Storm Atlas

Where the station shows one account, the Storm Atlas shows the whole population. It summarizes all 4,500 profiles into counts and percentages per weather state and renders them as a seven cell grid in severity order, each cell showing how many accounts sit in that condition right now. The headline above the grid names the state the pitch quotes (by default, storm warning) with the count behind it, and a scenario label makes clear whether you are looking at baseline conditions or after a specific shock, so the same grid answers "how many accounts are already in trouble" and "how many does this twist put in trouble".

Clicking a state drills down to the accounts behind the count (planned as a strip plot of runway within the selected state), which is how the demo moves from one judge-picked account to the population story: the atlas is fed by the same `profiles.json` and aggregates as everything else, so the headline number and the account cards can never disagree. The summary math lives in a pure module (`summarizeStormAtlas`, `accountsInState`) with unit tests, and the grid component is presentational: it reads counts, never recomputes them.

input.newString:
## Use of Solana

Solana provides the provenance layer for the findings: a tamper-evident, independently checkable record that the exact analysis we presented is the analysis we ran. The integration is deliberately small (memo transactions only, locked scope in `docs/decisions.md`), and it runs entirely on devnet.

How it works:

- **What goes on chain is digests, never data.** A memo transaction carries the SHA256 hash of the frozen `findings.json` (and the model card hash, plus an aggregate fingerprint over the published F1 table with the note "aggregates only, no raw rows"). No account id, no balance, no row of customer data ever appears in a transaction. The chain pins the identity of the artifact; the artifact itself stays in the repo.
- **The send path is audited, not improvised.** `scripts/solana/send_memo.py` refuses to sign until it has confirmed the endpoint is genuine Solana devnet (genesis hash assertion), sends the memo, confirms the transaction, reads the text back from the chain, verifies it matches byte for byte, and writes an evidence file with the signature and explorer URL. A known test string with a recorded digest lets us self-test the whole path before touching the real file.
- **The site never touches the network.** Evidence JSONs are bundled into `public/data/` at build time and rendered by a static receipt badge ("Anchored on Solana devnet, verified" when the read-back confirmed, "anchored at build time, signature: ..." otherwise). Zero runtime RPC calls, so the demo works with the booth wifi off and there is no wallet, no Anchor program, and no tokens anywhere in the project.
- **Why it earns the track claim.** The findings freeze and the chain anchor happen at the same moment: the number you show a judge and the hash on chain are the same bytes. Anyone can re-run `shasum -a 256 public/data/findings.json` in our repo, compare it to the explorer transaction, and verify we did not quietly recompute after judging.

The receipt badge component and evidence bundling are scaffolded; the anchor transaction is sent against the frozen artifacts during the competition-day sequence described in `docs/solana.md`.

# Storm Atlas Visualization Menu: 12 Ideas

Framing note before the menu: the seven weather states are `clear, cloudy, overcast, rain, drought, storm, flood`, severity runs `flood > storm > drought > rain > overcast > cloudy > clear`, and `drought` is the structural shortfall state (income covers 65 percent or less of spending even though runway is still 3.0 months and up). That drought state is a gift for metaphor: a dry map is not the same as a flooded map, and the two failure modes deserve different pictures.

## Family A: Precipitation as Data

### A1. Cohort Rainfield
- **One line**: A pixel sky where falling drops are cohorts of accounts, so the population literally rains harder as the twist lands.
- **Data reads**: `profiles.json` state counts via `summarizeStormAtlas` (which runs the parity `weatherState` ladder over `runway_state`, `runway_deci_months`, `buffer_cents`, income versus spending); scenario variants from `aggregates.json` preset twist summaries.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Every drop is 25 accounts. At baseline it drizzles. Under the standard EI twist the sky opens up and 1 in N of you is standing in it."
- **Style fit**: Perfect. This is the product's weather identity amplified. Okabe-Ito state colors on drop sprites, Terraria pixel sky, CSS keyframes only for drift, Canvas 2D for the drops.
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. Canvas 2D rain layer is already budgeted at 150 drops in prior research (citations 248 to 250), so no new technical risk. Offline safe. Reduced motion renders a static drop field with density still encoding counts. Projector risk: rain reads at thumbnail size but exact counts do not, so the printed count grid must stay visible. No conflict with the Three.js rejection or the SVG budget. Weakness: particle counts are an impression, not a measurement, so the legend must say "one drop is N accounts" and the exact numbers live in the grid beside it.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate** as the atmosphere layer, never as the only chart.

### A2. Population Rain Gauge (Reservoir of Resilience)
- **One line**: A big pixel gauge on the side of the atlas that fills to the share of the population surviving each scenario, and drains as shocks stack.
- **Data reads**: `aggregates.json` "share surviving each of the three example shocks" and "share with buffer <= 0"; `profiles.json` for the baseline fill level.
- **Pitch sentence**: "This is the population's resilience reservoir. Job loss alone drains it this far. Add the bills shock and it drops below the danger line."
- **Style fit**: Excellent. A gauge is weather station canon, a rain gauge is literally a meteorological instrument, and a fill level is the most projector-legible encoding there is. Pixel fill with wave animation, colored by severity band, danger line printed on the glass.
- **Honest cost**: 1 to 2 hours, the cheapest idea on this menu. SVG arc or rect fill, nowhere near the node budget. Fully offline. Reduced motion gives a static fill. The only honest work is defining the fill metric exactly once (surviving share, or aggregate buffer) and printing that definition on the gauge, because a gauge that quietly changes meaning is dishonest.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate**, best value per hour on the menu. Pair with anything.

### A3. Population Isotype ("1 in N" pixel people)
- **One line**: A grid of 100 tiny pixel characters under a sky, with exactly N of them standing under storm clouds, next to the giant "1 in N" headline.
- **Data reads**: `summarizeStormAtlas` headline count and `oneInN` over `profiles.json`; scenario label from the twist caller (same honest `scenarioLabel` contract the scaffold already has).
- **Pitch sentence**: "One in five accounts is one storm warning away from empty. Here they are."
- **Style fit**: Perfect. Isotype pictograms are the oldest honest population chart there is and pixel characters are native to the aesthetic. Each figure carries state color plus icon shape (the redundancy rule from citations 233 to 235).
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. 100 SVG figures is nothing against the 1,000 to 2,000 node comfort range. Fully offline. Reduced motion: static array. Thumbnail legibility is the best on this menu: a stranger understands "1 in 5" at 320 pixels wide. Only caveat is rounding: `oneInN` is a rounded divisor, so the array must show the exact count too (for example 912 of 4,500) or the picture and the sentence can drift by one figure.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate**, specifically as the headline and video surface.

## Family B: Geography Without Pretending

### B1. District Storm Cartogram
- **One line**: All 77 named districts as a grid of pixel tiles, each shaded by its share of accounts in storm or worse, arranged by region bands so it reads as a country without lying about shapes.
- **Data reads**: `districts.csv` (`district_id`, `district_name`, `region`, `inhabitants`, `unemployment_rate_2023`, `average_salary`); `accounts.csv` membership via `district_id` (already joined into `profiles.json`); per district state shares from the proposed `atlas.json` precompute.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Storms cluster. The districts with the highest unemployment hold the deepest storm cells, and that is where the plan engine should point its help."
- **Style fit**: Very good. A tile grid is honest pixel art cartography (the grid cartogram tradition: one tile, one district, area not distorted by geography). Region bands give the eye a macro shape. Legend printed as a pixel map key.
- **Honest cost**: 4 to 6 hours, the biggest idea here. 77 tiles plus labels is comfortably inside SVG budget. Fully offline. Reduced motion: no animation needed, static shading. Projector and thumbnail: excellent, a map is the single most legible shape on a screen. Risks: (1) we have district membership but no coordinates, so the tile layout must be declared as "arranged by region, not by geography" in the printed legend; (2) the Discovery claim "storms cluster where unemployment is high" must be verified in the Python precompute before we say it out loud, and if it does not hold we pivot the copy to whatever the frozen numbers actually say; (3) per district shares are new aggregates, so they ship from the engine build with a checksum, never computed in the browser. No conflict with prior decisions. District 69 has missing 2022 values, so the tile must render "no data" honestly, not zero.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate** and my recommended E5 hero.

### B2. Storm Share vs Unemployment Scatter
- **One line**: A 77 dot scatter, x is district unemployment, y is district storm share, with the outlier districts named in pixel callout boxes.
- **Data reads**: `districts.csv` `unemployment_rate_2023` (and `average_salary`, `crimes_2023` as alternates); per district storm share from `atlas.json`.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Run the regression in your head: the districts losing jobs in 2023 are the same districts where our accounts run out of runway first."
- **Style fit**: Moderate. It is a chart, not weather, but pixel dot sprites and a hand-drawn trend line keep it in the world. Best shown as a small companion panel next to the cartogram, not as the hero.
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours for the chart, plus the same `atlas.json` precompute as B1. 77 dots in SVG, trivial. Offline safe. Static under reduced motion. Risk: this is a correlation claim and Discovery is 35 percent of the rubric, so the sentence must be worded as correlation, never causation, and the frozen numbers must actually support it. One dot per district also hides population size, so dot size could encode `inhabitants` with a printed size legend.
- **Verdict**: **Viable with caveats**, and only if the precompute confirms the story. It is the strongest Discovery play on the menu.

### B3. Region Band Forecast
- **One line**: The bank's original regions rendered as horizontal weather bands, each band showing its own mini forecast of the seven states, like a regional forecast table on the evening news.
- **Data reads**: `districts.csv` `region`; `atlas.json` per region state shares; `aggregates.json` for the scenario dimension.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Here is the regional forecast: the north is cloudy, the capital is clear, and the industrial belt is already under a storm warning."
- **Style fit**: Good, TV forecast tables are instantly familiar and pixel friendly.
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. Fewer than 10 regions, so SVG is trivial. Offline, reduced motion safe, projector legible. The honest gap: regions have very unequal account counts, so every band needs its N printed, and the "forecast" wording must not imply we predict the future (it is a snapshot of the shipped year, the label should say "current conditions by region" or similar).
- **Verdict**: **Viable with caveats**, good cheap fallback if the cartogram is cut for time.

## Family C: 3D Bars

### C1. Isometric Pixel Bar Field (fake 3D)
- **One line**: A seven bar isometric skyline where bar height is accounts per state, drawn as stacked pixel blocks with skewed top faces, like a SimCity skyline of the population's weather.
- **Data reads**: `summarizeStormAtlas` counts over `profiles.json`, or `aggregates.json` per scenario for a before and after skyline.
- **Pitch sentence**: "This is our population's weather skyline, and here is the same skyline after the twist: the storm tower triples."
- **Style fit**: Great. Isometric pixel art is the native 3D of the Terraria and Stardew world, and a stacked block bar (each block = 50 accounts) is both a bar chart and a voxel toy.
- **Honest cost**: 3 to 4 hours, done as SVG polygons or CSS transforms with `skewY` and `scaleY` for the top faces. This is fake 3D in flat 2D, so it respects the Three.js rejection rather than reopening it, keeps SVG node counts low (7 bars times maybe 30 blocks each is about 210 nodes), stays offline and reduced-motion friendly. Legibility caveat: isometric heights are harder to compare than flat bars, so the exact count prints on each tower face and the flat seven cell grid stays visible as the honest reference. If someone wants real 3D with camera orbit, that is a Three.js reopening at 3 to 6 hours plus booth hardware risk with zero data-viz gain over the fake version, which prior research already rejected on exactly those grounds. My recommendation: do not reopen it, the fake isometric delivers the same picture.
- **Verdict**: **Viable with caveats**, genuinely fun and video-friendly, but it must carry printed numbers to stay honest.

### C2. True 3D Bar Scene (Three.js)
- **One line**: A real WebGL 3D bar chart with camera orbit and lighting.
- **Data reads**: same as C1.
- **Pitch sentence**: same as C1.
- **Style fit**: Looks flashy in a thumbnail.
- **Honest cost**: 3 to 6 hours plus a WebGL dependency, exactly the profile prior research rejected: booth hardware risk, no data-viz benefit over C1, and it breaks the "charts stay DOM and SVG" architecture rule. Reduced motion and offline are handleable but the risk budget is not.
- **Verdict**: **Fun but skip.** C1 buys the same picture for half the cost and none of the risk.

## Family D: Distributions and Flows

### D1. Ridgeline Shift (baseline versus twist)
- **One line**: Two overlapping pixel ridgeline curves of the runway distribution, baseline and post-twist, with the storm threshold wall drawn through both, so you watch the whole population slide left.
- **Data reads**: `aggregates.json` "runway distributions under each preset twist"; threshold values from the printed `weatherState` ladder (storm at 3.0 months, flood at 0).
- **Pitch sentence**: "The twist does not just hurt the weakest accounts. It slides the entire population toward the wall."
- **Style fit**: Good. Ridgelines read like mountain ranges on a weather map, fill with state colors near the threshold, and the "wall" at 3.0 months can be drawn as a pixel cliff with warning tape.
- **Honest cost**: 3 to 4 hours. Both curves are maybe 40 to 60 path points each, trivial SVG. Offline and reduced motion safe (a CSS clip reveal is the only motion). Projector legibility is decent but the concept is more abstract than a map or gauge, so it needs one big annotation sentence on the canvas. It consumes the same frozen distribution data the histograms need, so it and D3 share plumbing.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate** as the twist storytelling surface. This is the clearest "the twist moves everyone" picture on the menu.

### D2. Storm Front Migration (state to state flow)
- **One line**: Seven weather stations connected by curved arrows whose thickness is how many accounts travel from each baseline state to each shocked state, so the twist becomes a storm front crossing the map.
- **Data reads**: `profiles.json` twice conceptually (baseline state and state after `applyTwist` for the preset), shipped as a 7 by 7 transition matrix in `atlas.json`; `aggregates.json` for scenario labels.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Watch the front pass: 600 accounts left cloudy and never came back. They are in storm now."
- **Style fit**: Excellent metaphor, weather fronts are arrows on every TV forecast. Pixel arrow sprites, state colors, motion along the arrow paths.
- **Honest cost**: 4 to 6 hours, the riskiest strong idea. The 7 by 7 matrix has at most 49 flows, but naive curves will clutter, so flows need filtering to the top N plus an "other" bucket with a printed note. The transition matrix is a new derived artifact and must come from the engine build (same parity ladder, checksummed), never from the UI re-twisting 4,500 accounts live. Reduced motion renders static arrows with thickness only. Offline safe. It competes with the architecture's planned strip plot drill-down for the same screen slot.
- **Verdict**: **Viable with caveats.** High storytelling reward, real build cost, and it needs Q1 answered yes.

### D3. Runway Histogram with Storm Threshold Wall
- **One line**: A pixel histogram of all 4,500 accounts by runway bucket, with the storm and flood walls drawn as warning tape lines and every bar stacked by state color.
- **Data reads**: `aggregates.json` runway distributions (or bucketed in the precompute from `runway_deci_months` and `runway_state` in `profiles.json`).
- **Pitch sentence**: "This many accounts live to the left of this wall, and the wall is where the warnings start."
- **Style fit**: Good, bars as stacked pixel blocks, tape lines as NWS style hazard stripes (citation 233 colors).
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. 20 to 25 buckets in SVG, trivial. Offline, reduced motion safe, projector friendly with printed bar totals. Honest detail: `no_shortfall` accounts sit at the artificial 120.0 month cap, so the right-most bucket must be labeled "no shortfall" and not drawn as a real 120 month runway.
- **Verdict**: **Viable with caveats**, an honest workhorse, less unique than D1.

### D4. State Drill-Down Strip Plot (the architecture's planned one)
- **One line**: Clicking an atlas cell opens a beeswarm strip of just that state's accounts along the runway axis, so one cell's count becomes individual faces.
- **Data reads**: `accountsInState` from `stormAtlas.ts` over `profiles.json` (`runway_deci_months`, `account_id`, flags), exactly as the scaffold docstring already anticipates.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Every dot behind this number is a household. Pick one and we will run it live."
- **Style fit**: Good, dots as pixel weather icons along a runway signpost axis, which reuses the account-level signpost money shot language.
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. Critical sizing note: the largest state can hold well over 1,000 accounts, so the strip plot is either Canvas 2D (fine) or SVG with sub-sampling plus a printed "showing 800 of 2,412" note. This is the sanctioned drill-down in `docs/architecture.md`, so it is the lowest-politics choice and it feeds the judge-picked account flow directly.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate** for the drill-down slot regardless of which hero we pick above.

## Family E: Synoptics

### E1. Scenario Forecast Row (the "five day forecast")
- **One line**: Five pixel forecast cards in a row: Baseline, Laid off, Bills up 15%, Furnace repair, Combo, each with a weather icon, the survival share, and a tiny gauge.
- **Data reads**: `aggregates.json` preset twist summaries (the four presets plus baseline); `shockPresets.ts` labels for exact wording parity.
- **Pitch sentence**: "Here is the whole population's five day forecast. Day one is today. Day five is what happens if the wrong week hits."
- **Style fit**: Perfect. It is a literal TV forecast row, and it maps one-to-one onto the four shipped presets, so no new scenario vocabulary is invented.
- **Honest cost**: 2 to 3 hours. Pure cards and small SVG icons, no motion needed, offline safe, very projector legible. The honesty guard: the row must be labeled as scenarios over the shipped year, not predictions, and each card prints its scenario label verbatim from the preset module so the words can never drift from what the engine ran.
- **Verdict**: **Strong candidate** as a compact support surface, and a natural header for the atlas during the live twist.

### E2. Almanac Page (12 month population normals)
- **One line**: A pixel almanac spread of the population's median balance across the 12 shipped months, styled like a farmer's almanac climate page.
- **Data reads**: `profiles.json` `balance_series` (12 rows of `avg_daily_balance` per account), aggregated to monthly population medians in the precompute.
- **Pitch sentence**: "The population has a climate, not just a weather: the late-winter dip is when districts get dangerous."
- **Style fit**: Lovely and on brand (the almanac is weather culture).
- **Honest cost**: 3 to 4 hours plus precompute. Legibility is fine, but the story competes with the twist narrative, and the pitch has only 60 seconds. The seasonal claim would also need the frozen numbers to actually show it.
- **Verdict**: **Fun but skip** for this weekend. File it as E5-plus if time remains.

# Ranked Shortlist: Top 3 to Present

**1. B1 District Storm Cartogram, with B2 scatter as its side panel.**
This is the hero. It gives the Storm Atlas its name: an actual atlas. Seventy-seven real named districts in one pixel tile grid, shaded by share of accounts in storm or worse, arranged by region with a printed legend that says "arranged by region, not to geography." It is the most projector-legible shape on the menu, it is the only idea that turns our unused `districts.csv` demographics into a Discovery-grade finding ("storms cluster where unemployment is high", pending precompute verification), and it composes with the existing seven cell grid rather than replacing it: the grid becomes the printed mapping legend and the counts table beneath the map, exactly where a real weather map puts its key. Clicking a tile can reuse `accountsInState` style drill-down to jump to a district's accounts, which hands the judge-picked account flow its entry point. Cost is honest at 4 to 6 hours plus a 30 to 45 minute Python precompute, all inside decisions we already made: 77 SVG tiles, no WebGL, no network.

**2. A2 Population Rain Gauge plus A1 Cohort Rainfield, sold as one "precipitation" package.**
This is the live-twist surface. During the 3 minute judge twist, the gauge drains and the rain intensifies as the scenario changes, so the population consequence of the judge's shock is felt in one second without anyone reading a number. The gauge (1 to 2 hours) is the measured layer with the survival share printed on the glass; the rainfield (2 to 3 hours, already-budgeted Canvas 2D at 150 drops) is the felt layer with its "one drop is N accounts" legend. It plays beautifully behind the existing seven cell grid, which stays the honest numbers backbone. Both survive reduced motion as static states, both are offline, both fit the 120 second video as background texture under the narration.

**3. A3 Population Isotype "1 in N" pixel people.**
This is the pitch and thumbnail surface. For the 1 minute opening, one image carries the headline: 100 pixel characters, N of them under storm clouds, the giant "1 in N" beside the exact count (for example 912 of 4,500) so rounding never lies. It is 2 to 3 hours, 100 SVG nodes, and it is the single most thumbnail-legible object we can build. It also doubles as the atlas headline cell: mount it directly above or inside the seven cell grid, where the grid's first cell visually continues into the pictogram.

How they combine: the grid stays mounted as legend and counts, the isotype headlines it, the cartogram maps it, the gauge and rain animate it during the twist, and D4's strip plot handles drill-down. If only one ships, ship the cartogram. If two, add the isotype.

Alternates if Q1 (precompute) comes back no: swap B1 for B3 (Region Band Forecast) and D1 stays droppable; A2, A3, and E1 all need no new precompute and are safe regardless.

# The Population Money Shot (video thumbnail frame)

**Single recommendation: B1's "front crossing the atlas" moment.** At the instant the twist lands, the 77 tiles cascade their severity colors from the clear end of the ladder toward storm and flood in a wave, the headline "1 in N accounts hits storm warning under the standard EI twist" is already locked on screen, and the printed legend is visible in frame. It is the population twin of the account-level money shot (storm boundary mid transition, signpost runway number): same motion grammar, one scale up. It reads at thumbnail size as "a map getting hit by a storm," which no bar chart can do, and the freeze frame at the mid-cascade instant is both beautiful and honest because the end state is one click away.

Guard rails for the shot: the cascade is presentation of precomputed counts, so the freeze frame must show the exact headline count in text; under `prefers-reduced-motion` the app skips the cascade and renders the end state instantly, and the video recording runbook is where motion is legitimately enabled; the video shot list in `docs/video/shots.md` needs one new clip slot and a thumbnail extraction at the mid-cascade timestamp.

Fallback if the cartogram is cut for time: the A3 isotype under the A1 downpour at max intensity, headline overlaid. Same one-second read, less unique.

# Honesty Checklist Note

- **Printed mapping legend**: B1 (mandatory: tile meaning, shading scale, "arranged by region, not to geography", and the district 69 missing data marker), B2 (axis definitions, dot size legend if used), B3 (per band N printed). A1 needs its "one drop is N accounts" key even though it is not a map. A2 needs the fill metric defined on the gauge face.
- **Numbers from bundled artifacts only**: every count on screen comes from `summarizeStormAtlas` over shipped `profiles.json` (the parity ladder precedent the scaffold already sets), or from `aggregates.json` and the proposed `atlas.json`, both built and checksummed by `scripts/engine/build.py`. Zero runtime computation of anything that was not shipped. Everything stays offline, which these all do since they are bundled JSON reads plus pure render.
- **Never recompute judge metrics in the UI**: three-tier rule to keep straight. (1) Shipped judge metrics (income, spending, buffer, runway, and the rest) are never touched, re-derived, or re-shocked in the browser, so D2's transition matrix and B1's district shares ship precomputed from Python that mirrors the golden fixtures. (2) Counting states through the `weatherState` parity ladder is allowed, precedent set by `stormAtlas.ts`. And the B2 correlation sentence says correlation, never causation, and only after the frozen numbers confirm it.
